Listen to this article Share Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, the minister of Interior, and the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) have asked the Federal High Court in Abuja to dismiss a suit seeking the disclosure of records relating to the minister’s participation in the mandatory one-year national service scheme. In separate court processes, the minister and the NYSC opposed the suit filed by the Incorporated Trustees of Pathway to Equity and Charity Foundation, which seeks to compel the release of documents relating to Tunji-Ojo’s national service and his primary assignment at the Federal Capital Territory Administration (FCTA). The NYSC, in its counter-affidavit, said the minister completed his national service in 2019/2020 following remobilisation, rather than in 2006 as referenced in the foundation’s case. The matter came up on Thursday before Justice Salim Ibrahim, but hearing could not proceed after Solo Akuna, SAN, counsel to the foundation, applied orally for an adjournment to enable him respond to the minister’s application to be joined as a respondent. Justice Ibrahim adjourned the matter until December 7 for hearing. In the suit marked FHC/ABJ/CS/1812/2026, the foundation is seeking an order of mandamus compelling the NYSC to disclose documents supporting the minister’s claim that he completed the mandatory national service. It also wants the court to direct the FCTA, the second respondent, to produce records showing that Tunji-Ojo undertook his primary assignment. Tunji-Ojo, through a motion on notice filed by his lawyer, Abiola Olaniyi, sought to be joined as the third respondent and asked the court to dismiss the suit. He also sought an order dissolving the foundation, registered under number 9696061, on the grounds that it had acted outside the objectives and provisions of its constitution. The minister argued that the foundation, registered under Part F of the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020, was established as a non-profit and non-political organisation and was bound by its constitution. He contended that instituting the action amounted to engaging in political activities outside the scope of its registered objectives and constitutional powers. Relying on Sections 823(1) and 825(1)(b) of CAMA 2020, Tunji-Ojo argued that the foundation had contravened the law by undertaking activities inconsistent with its stated objectives. Read also: Alonso demands Chelsea response ahead of Forest clash He urged the court to grant his applications in the interest of justice and public policy. The NYSC also asked the court to dismiss the suit, arguing that it had provided the foundation with the available records relating to the minister’s service. In a counter-affidavit deposed to by Emmanuel Tsamya, a litigation secretary in the corps’ Legal Unit, the NYSC said some of the claims in the foundation’s affidavit were not within its knowledge. Tsamya said the corps could confirm that Tunji-Ojo undertook national service and completed his primary assignment at the FCTA, but disputed the reference to 2006. According to him, the minister undertook his national service in 2019/2020 following remobilisation. The NYSC said it generally maintained records of corps members who participated in and completed the scheme, but some documents might not be immediately available due to circumstances such as relocation of office accommodation. Tsamya said the foundation’s letter dated July 22 was received by the corps on July 23, after which the FCT secretariat forwarded the available documents to the Director-General. He said further inquiries at the Abuja secretariat showed that several records had been lost during previous office relocations, leaving the documents supplied as the only available records relating to the minister. The corps said it responded through a letter dated August 24, with reference number NYSC/LEG/FOI/VOL.1/2026/61, and sent the available documents to the foundation through the email address provided by its solicitors. Tsamya said an earlier attempt to deliver the documents physically on August 27 failed because the address supplied by the solicitors could not be traced and their telephone number was unreachable. He said the documents were eventually delivered on October 20 to Amaka Isiguzo, secretary to the foundation’s solicitors, at an alternative location provided after a telephone conversation with the lawyer. According to the NYSC, the documents released included the minister’s personal details on the 2006 Batch B database, the list of corps members deployed to the FCT during the batch, his application for remobilisation dated September 6, 2019, and the corresponding application records. Other documents included a receipt for the refund of allowances previously received, the remobilisation letter, camp registration slip, 2019 Batch C biodata page and monthly clearance records for the 2019/2020 service year. The corps also listed a letter dated October 18, 2022, forwarding a request for the issuance of a certificate of national service, the certificate bearing number A004523631 and dated February 28, 2023, and the certificate issuance register. However, Tsamya said the foundation, in a subsequent letter dated October 27, complained that only two of the eight categories of documents requested had been released. The foundation also alleged that the copies supplied were blurred and not certified. The NYSC argued that the foundation had already received the available records and had not established grounds for the court to grant the reliefs sought. He urged the court to dismiss the suit in its entirety. The court is expected to hear the substantive applications on December 7.
